title: Climatic Persistence of Lardizabala biternata, an Endemic Chilean Vine with Agronomic Potential Under Climate Change
content: Climate change may reshape the climatic suitability of many plant species, yet its ef-fects on wild native resources with agronomic potential remain poorly understood. Lardizabala biternata is a monotypic vine endemic to Chile that produces edible fruits, remains uncultivated, and occurs in a biodiversity hotspot exposed to land-use change and climatic drying. We used a curated occurrence database, spatial thinning, biocli-matic predictor selection, and an ensemble Species Distribution Modeling (SDM) framework to estimate historical and future climatic suitability for L. biternata in cen-tral–southern Chile. Future suitability was projected for 2021–2040, 2041–2060, and 2061–2080 under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 3-7.0 (SSP3-7.0), a medium-to-high emissions pathway. Binary suitable/unsuitable maps were compared with the histori-cal baseline to quantify areas of suitability persistence, gain, and loss, as well as latitu-dinal centroid shifts. The retained models showed strong discriminatory performance, with Area Under the Curve (AUC) values of 0.88. Suitability was mainly associated with humid and thermally buffered conditions. Projections indicated high climatic persistence, very low losses, limited gains, and a gradual southward centroid shift of approximately 51.77 km by 2061–2080. These findings suggest that L. biternata may retain substantial suitable climatic areas under future climate change, supporting its evaluation as an underutilized native fruit resource for germplasm safeguarding, ex situ conservation, and conservation-oriented cultivation.
